title: A Math Professor and NFL Player Who Says He Was Just Lucky
dek: John Urschel played in the NFL while finishing an MIT math PhD, yet says talent is only a small part of it — his success came from "an enormous amount of hard work" and luck. He even hopes his football fame did not get him his MIT job.
why: This is the audio version of a video interview, so the information density is not high, but Urschel explaining how he crammed two full-time jobs into the same week, and why he ultimately gave up football, is worth hearing.
who: Suited to founders and engineers interested in "doing two hard things at once," especially those who want to know how to fit two full-time jobs into one week and when to give one of them up.
skip: The first two minutes or so of childhood and family background can be skipped; start listening from the coach's talk at 08:16.

points.h: A coach's joke made him realize he could make the NFL
points.body: After Urschel's junior season, his position coach called him in, essentially saying, "Don't think about anything crazy, stay another year" — crazy meaning declaring early for the draft. He hadn't been thinking about the NFL at all, but that remark made him realize for the first time: this would happen if he wanted it. Later the coach would say in practice, "They (the league) will like this move." He wasn't running on self-confidence; he was running on others assuming he belonged at that level.

points.h: He asked his coach about a PhD; the coach thought he already had one
points.body: Urschel was doing an MIT math PhD while playing in the NFL, and he says he "didn't cheat," because he asked coach John Harbaugh in advance whether he could go back to school for a degree. The coach replied, "Absolutely, we support players finishing their education," then a minute later added a text: "I thought you already had a degree and a master's." Urschel replied, "But I don't have a PhD." The coach replied, "Oh, OK," and that was the approval. He deliberately picked courses with no exams that he could pass by reading the textbook — three PhD courses in one semester.

points.h: On planes he had to pretend his math book was a chess book
points.body: During the NFL season almost all his time each day went to football, with film study at night. Math could only be done in the time others used to relax — for example on team flights, when everyone was watching movies. He says if he were reading a chess book it would be completely fine, but reading a math book was "a little suspicious," and teammates might think he was too distracted, so he would say, "It's not a math book, it's a chess book," flip it open for them, and they would say, "OK." The real solution was that he finished the textbook before the semester even started; otherwise it would have been impossible.

points.h: The CTE controversy conveniently gave him cover to retire
points.body: The host asked whether the years when CTE (brain damage from repeated head hits) became an NFL headline were exactly when he was considering retirement. Urschel said, "It gave me very good cover." But he also says he was worried before that. He was weighing whether to play another season — the last year of his rookie contract, with the next contract worth at least a million dollars a year, while his first-year base salary was 420,000. He once convinced himself to stay with "there's one year left on the contract, I'll honor it" — the same mindset as when he honored his commitment to Penn State.

points.h: Looking back, he doesn't know what he was agonizing over
points.body: Urschel says looking back, agonizing over retirement made little sense: the team could cut him at any time, the contract wasn't guaranteed, and an injury would end it. What he really cared about was math and his newborn child, and both were growing more important, while football ranked third yet was a real burden on the first two — not just the head, but the whole body, whether he could still walk at 50, whether he could pick up his grandchildren and his daughter. He says, "I needed to retire, focus on math, and go be with my kid."

points.h: He estimates only 4% of Americans like math
points.body: The host asked him to guess how many out of 100 Americans like math, and Urschel said that if you define "math" the way the general public understands it, 4% might even be high. The host said that number was a little sad. Urschel's own definition is very broad: math is the quantitative language we all share for reasoning about problems, and engineering, theoretical physics, statistics and theoretical computer science all count as math — not far from doing puzzles, not far from the goal of "understanding something."

points.h: His daughter won't play football; his son must truly need it
points.body: Asked whether his two children should play football, Urschel said his daughter should not — that level of risk he won't accept. For his son, if it looks like something he "really needs to do," he would allow it. He explains what needing means: football suits young people who crave it and can benefit from "consensual violence, controlled, agreed-upon aggression" — with rules, not trying to hurt people, essentially a proxy for war. He says it was very good for the combative high schooler he once was. If it's just "because Dad played" or "because all my friends play," he would first have the kid try wrestling or judo.

points.h: He says he actually had no talent as an NFL player
points.body: The host praised him for being good at several hard things at once, and Urschel said talent does play a role, but compared with NFL players he "had no talent" — he admits he has some athletic gifts, like broad shoulders, but in the league that doesn't count. So how did he succeed? "Hard work, an enormous amount of hard work." The source is "wanting to be better." Asked whether his MIT job came from football fame, he said, "I don't know, I hope not."
